transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, to be perfectly honest with you, doctor, I'm only sitting in this chair because the stress of my situation has been mounting, and my family thinks I need to "talk to someone" about it. But the stress isn't just coming out of nowhere. I’m here because for over a year now—fourteen months, really, ever since the department restructuring last October—I’ve been trying to get someone, anyone, to take seriously what is actually happening to me at work. 

I’m a computer support specialist. I have my bachelor's degree, I’ve been doing this for decades, so I know exactly how backend systems operate. I know the difference between standard automation and manual manipulation. And this new ticket rotation system they implemented? Along with these sudden, supposedly "random" security audits? I know for an absolute fact they are being used to build a paper trail against me. Specifically against me. They purposefully route the most impossible, undocumented legacy network issues into my queue right before the audit scripts trigger. It's mathematically impossible for it to be a coincidence. 

I've tried to explain this. I've sat down with management, I've brought them my own tracking sheets and routing headers to show the discrepancies, and they just... they patronize me. They keep showing me these sanitized server logs and saying, "Oh, it’s just policy, the algorithm distributes the tickets evenly, you're doing fine." But I know what I'm looking at. They are quietly trying to manufacture a reason to terminate me, and nobody will just look at the actual evidence I've gathered.
Do you think anyone else is in on this alleged plot against you at work?

Well, no, I... I want to be very clear about this, because I know exactly how it sounds when people talk about these sorts of workplace issues, and I am a very logical person. I don't make leaps without proof. So, no, I'm not saying the whole building is out to get me or that there's some massive company-wide conspiracy. I don't have any evidence of that. 

You know, I look at the guys sitting in the cubicles next to me—guys I've worked with for, gosh, going on twelve, maybe fifteen years now in some cases—and they're just trying to get through their shift. They complain about the new ticketing interface just as much as I do, though of course, they aren't seeing the same impossible legacy errors dumped into their queues. I've checked. I've glanced at their dashboards when I walk by to get coffee, just to establish a baseline, and their ticket loads are perfectly normal. Standard distribution. 

So, no, I don't think my peers are in on it. They wouldn't even have the administrative privileges to manipulate the backend routing anyway. It has to be coming from the top down. The department heads, the ones who pushed this restructuring last October and brought in the new software. I haven't been able to isolate any other specific individuals because, well, the system is designed to mask manual overrides as automated load-balancing. They hide behind the algorithm. So I can't sit here and give you a list of names of coworkers or anything like that. I just know what the data tells me, and the data says whoever controls the audit scripts is the one doing it. But as far as anyone else being involved? No. I haven't seen anything to suggest that.
Have you considered the possibility that your interpretation of the data might be incorrect?

Incorrect? No, doctor, I... look, I understand why you're asking that. It’s the obvious question, right? "Is the IT guy just reading too much into a software glitch?" And I have asked myself that, believe me. I mean, I’m a professional. I’ve been doing this for decades. When a system throws an anomaly, the very first thing you do—the *first* thing—is check your own assumptions. You check the physical layer, you check the network layer, you check the application layer. You rule out user error. My error. 

So, yes, when this started happening a little over a year ago—fourteen months, to be precise, right after that department restructuring—I initially thought, "Okay, maybe I’m misunderstanding the new load-balancing protocol." I spent weekends, actual weekends off the clock, reading the documentation for the new ticket rotation system. I ran simulations. I built spreadsheets tracking the exact timestamp of every legacy issue routed to my queue versus the exact timestamp of the security audit scripts triggering. 

And the thing is, I’ve tried to show this to them! I’ve literally sat in management's office, laid out the routing headers, pointed to the discrepancies, and said, "Look at this correlation." And they just... they smile that tight little HR smile, and they pull up their own sanitized server logs. They slide them across the desk and tell me, "Oh, it’s just policy, the algorithm distributes the tickets evenly, you're doing fine." 

But they aren't looking at the raw data! They're looking at the dashboard summaries, which are easily manipulated if you have administrative access. I know they are using this new ticket rotation and these audits to build a paper trail against me. I know it. Because if my interpretation was incorrect, the math wouldn't hold up. But the math *does* hold up. The probability of these specific undocumented legacy errors hitting my queue precisely three to five minutes before an automated audit, over and over and over again for fourteen months, is statistically zero. So, no, my interpretation isn't incorrect. What's incorrect is management sitting there, looking me in the eye, and telling me it's "just policy" when the raw data proves they are targeting me. I just need someone, anyone, to actually look at the proof I've gathered and take this seriously.
Do you think it's possible that your feelings of being targeted are influencing how you interpret the data from the ticket rotation system?

Well, no, doctor, I... I don't think it's my feelings influencing the data, because the data came first. I didn't start out feeling targeted. I started out feeling confused, and then frustrated, and *then* the data showed me why I should feel targeted. 

You see, I’m a very analytical person. It’s what I’ve done for a living for decades. When I look at a dataset, I strip the emotion out of it. I don't look at a routing header and think, "Oh, this makes me feel bad." I look at a routing header and I see the timestamp, the origin IP, the destination queue, the protocol flags. It's binary. It's ones and zeros. And that's exactly why I'm sitting here in this chair today. 

Because for over a year now—fourteen months of this—I’ve been trying to get someone, anyone, to just sit down and look at the ones and zeros with me and take seriously what is actually happening. I'm telling you, this new ticket rotation system and these security audits, they are being used to build a paper trail against me at work. I didn't invent that idea out of thin air because I was feeling insecure. The data led me to that conclusion. 

And it's maddening, it really is, because I've gone to management with this. I've scheduled the meetings, I've brought the spreadsheets, I've highlighted the impossible correlation between the legacy errors hitting my queue and the audit scripts firing. And they just sit there, and they pull up their own logs—which, again, are dashboard summaries, not the raw data, and anyone with admin rights can sanitize a dashboard summary—and they keep showing me these logs and saying, "Oh, it’s just policy, the algorithm distributes the tickets evenly, you're doing fine." 

But how can they say that? How can they say it's just policy when the raw data clearly shows a targeted pattern? If it were just my feelings, I wouldn't have spreadsheets. I wouldn't have routing headers. I wouldn't have spent my weekends running simulations to prove it. I wouldn't be here, fourteen months later, still trying to get someone to understand that they are manufacturing a reason to get rid of me. It's not my feelings. It's the facts. And nobody will look at the facts.
Have you experienced any significant changes or stressful events in your personal life over the past fourteen months?

Stressful events? In my personal life? No. No, doctor, I... I want to be very clear about that, too, because I know how this might look from the outside. You might be sitting there thinking that maybe I am under some sort of immense stress at home and I am just projecting it onto the office, or bringing personal baggage into my workspace. But that is simply not the case. 

Outside of this entire manufactured nightmare with the ticket rotation and the audits, my life is... well, it is completely normal. It is stable. I still keep my house in immaculate order. I mean, I am the one who handles all the finances for us. I pay all the bills, and I don't just pay them haphazardly, I have a very rigorous spreadsheet system for tracking our household expenditures and utility fluctuations, making sure everything balances out to the penny at the end of every month. I help my wife with whatever she needs around the house. We actually just spent the weekend putting in a new raised garden bed in the backyard. I measured it all out for her, calculated the soil volume, set up a timed drip irrigation system so she wouldn't have to water it manually. So things at home are perfectly fine. There hasn't been any sort of disruption or life-changing event in the last fourteen months. 

And honestly, even at the office, if you separate out the targeted routing stuff and just look at my core duties, I still handle the technical parts of my job exactly as I always have. Flawlessly. Nobody, not even the management team trying to build this case against me, is coming to me and saying my actual technical work is sloppy. They can't say I am disorganized, because my resolutions are pristine. When I get a legitimate server migration issue or a user error that needs a remote desktop session, I fix it, and I document every single step of my troubleshooting in the log. My work is as sharp as it was on day one. So, no, there are no personal stressors or changes affecting me. It is solely this one, highly specific, data-proven situation at work.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep over the past fourteen months?

Sleep? No... no, I wouldn't say there have been any changes. I mean, I know exactly why you're asking. You're probably thinking, "Here's a guy who is dealing with a massive, targeted campaign against him at work, he must be tossing and turning all night." But that's... well, it's just not the case. 

I've always been very, very disciplined about my sleep hygiene. You have to be, in my line of work. If you're working on complex network architecture or, you know, parsing thousands of lines of raw server logs, cognitive fatigue is your worst enemy. A tired brain misses a misplaced semicolon, or misinterprets a timestamp. And I absolutely cannot afford to make a single mistake right now, not with management scrutinizing every move I make, waiting for me to slip up so they can justify their little paper trail. 

So, I keep a very strict schedule. I am in bed by 10:30 PM, without fail. I might read for twenty minutes or so—usually industry periodicals, keeping up with new load-balancing protocols, that sort of thing—and then it's lights out. I wake up at 5:45 AM. Every single day. Even on weekends. Now, sure, occasionally on a Saturday, if I'm running a really heavy data extraction to update my spreadsheets on those audit triggers we talked about, I might stay at the computer a bit later to watch the script finish compiling, but I always ensure I get my core seven hours. 

I don't lie awake worrying about this, doctor. I really don't. Because, like I said, I have the data. The math is entirely on my side. Usually, the people who lose sleep are the ones who are uncertain, or the ones who are lying. And I am neither. I know exactly what they are doing, and I have the documentation to prove it. So, no, my sleep is just as regular as it has always been.
Have you ever felt like you're observing yourself or your surroundings from outside your body?

Outside my body? Like... like floating above myself or something? No. No, doctor, I... I can safely say I have never experienced anything like that. I don't even really understand how that would work, to be honest with you, from a strictly physiological or neurological standpoint. 

I am a very grounded person. I am always right here, firmly in my own head, completely present in my physical space. I mean, I've read about things like that—people who do deep meditation or maybe have some sort of strange psychological break and they feel like they are watching themselves from the corner of the ceiling. But for me? Absolutely not. 

When I am sitting in my chair at the office, I am one hundred percent there. I feel the ergonomic mesh of the chair back, I know exactly where my hands are on the mechanical keyboard, I am acutely aware of the refresh rate on my dual monitors. I have to be. If I were floating around outside my body, or feeling disconnected from my physical surroundings, how could I possibly track the routing headers? How could I maintain the level of absolute, sustained focus required to document those audit triggers we were just talking about? 

My mind and my body are entirely synchronized. I don't lose time, I don't drift off into some ethereal plane, and I certainly don't watch myself from afar. I am firmly rooted in the real world, dealing with physical hardware, physical servers, and the very real, very tangible data they produce. If anything, I would argue that I am much more tuned in to my surroundings than most of the people I work with, because I actually have to pay attention to every single detail. I can't afford to be disconnected. So, no, I've never had any sort of out-of-body experience. I am always entirely present.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds that other people cannot hear?

Voices? You mean like auditory hallucinations? No, definitely not. I mean, I understand that in your profession, when someone comes in talking about a conspiracy—and I hate using that word because it implies something irrational, whereas what I'm dealing with is a documented, systemic issue—but when someone brings up a coordinated effort against them, you have to run through the checklist. You have to ask if they're hearing things, seeing things, losing touch with reality. I get it. It's standard diagnostic protocol. 

But no, I don't hear voices. The only voices I hear are the ones that are actually there. I hear my wife asking me to help with the groceries, I hear the hum of the HVAC unit cycling on and off, and I hear my manager, Dave, making his little passive-aggressive comments by the water cooler. That's it. 

I don't hear disembodied voices telling me to do things, or whispering my name when I'm alone in the server room. If I heard something like that, I would immediately assume it was a localized acoustic anomaly, maybe a cross-feed on the intercom system or a failing fan bearing on one of the blade servers. I wouldn't jump to the conclusion that it was a voice in my head. My brain doesn't work like that. I operate on logic, on empirical evidence. I analyze inputs and outputs. 

If I'm sitting at my desk and I hear a sound, I can trace it back to its source. I know the difference between the high-pitched whine of a failing hard drive and the normal operational hum of a healthy one. I know the sound of the cleaning crew's cart rolling down the hall on the floor above me. I am very attuned to my auditory environment, but only the actual, physical environment. 

There's no phantom chorus narrating my life or telling me that management is out to get me. I don't need voices to tell me that. I have the raw data. I have the server logs, the timestamp discrepancies, the routing algorithms that clearly show my ticket queue is being artificially inflated with the most complex, time-consuming issues while everyone else gets the simple password resets. I don't need to hear things that aren't there because the things that *are* there are more than enough to prove my case. The evidence is entirely tangible, completely silent, and sitting right there in my spreadsheets. So, no, doctor, no voices. Just the facts.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

Lost interest? Well, that's... I suppose that's a matter of perspective, isn't it? If you mean, do I still enjoy the things I used to enjoy, the answer is yes, absolutely. I haven't lost the capacity for enjoyment or the interest itself. It's more a question of time allocation and prioritization, given the current circumstances. 

Take my model trains, for example. I've been an N-scale enthusiast for over thirty years. It requires a tremendous amount of precision—laying the track, wiring the DCC controllers, ensuring the voltage drop across the layout is minimized so the locomotives run smoothly. It's highly technical, very satisfying work. I used to spend maybe ten, twelve hours a week down in the basement, working on the scenery or soldering feeder wires. I still love it. I still read the forums, I still keep up with the latest decoder releases from Digitrax. The interest is entirely intact. 

But have I actually run a train in the last, say, eight months? No. No, I haven't. But that's not because I don't want to. It's because I simply cannot afford the distraction right now. When I get home from work, after dealing with the constant, subtle sabotage of my ticket queue, I have to spend my evening analyzing the day's server logs. I have to cross-reference the timestamps on the tickets assigned to me against the general pool to prove the statistical anomaly of my workload. If I were down in the basement wiring a miniature crossing signal, I wouldn't be compiling the evidence I need to protect my job. 

So, it's not a loss of interest, doctor. It's a reallocation of resources. My cognitive bandwidth is currently entirely consumed by defending myself against this targeted campaign at work. I still enjoy reading about network architecture, too—I used to read RFCs for fun, believe it or not, just to understand the underlying protocols of the internet. But now, when I read technical documentation, it's strictly to find loopholes or audit trails that management might be using to manipulate my performance metrics. 

The enjoyment is still there, dormant, waiting for this whole situation to be resolved. Once I present my findings, once I expose what Dave and the rest of them are doing and clear my name, I'll go right back to the trains. I have a whole expansion planned for the freight yard. I just... I have to finish this data extraction first. I have to make sure my spreadsheets are bulletproof. So, no, I haven't lost interest in anything. I've just had to put my hobbies on hold because reality is demanding my full attention right now.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite over the past fourteen months?

Changes in my appetite? Over the past fourteen months... no. No, I wouldn't say that. I'm a creature of habit, doctor, a very strict creature of habit. I've basically been eating the exact same breakfast and lunch for... well, it has to be at least five or six years now. 

Every morning, 6:15 AM, I have half a cup of steel-cut oats, a handful of blueberries, and black coffee. Then for lunch, I pack a turkey sandwich on whole wheat—no mayo, just a little mustard—and an apple. Usually a Honeycrisp, if they're in season, or maybe a Fuji. And I eat it right at my desk. I have to, really. I mean, if I were to take a full hour in the breakroom, or go out to a restaurant like some of the younger guys do, that is exactly when the dispatch system would mysteriously route a cluster of high-priority, multi-layered network outage tickets directly to my queue. It's just too predictable. Dave knows when the standard lunch hour is, so I just bypass the whole vulnerability. I eat at my desk while keeping one eye on the incoming ticket feed and the other on my diagnostic tools. 

But as for the food itself, and my actual desire to eat it? Completely unchanged. I still get hungry right around 11:45 AM, just like clockwork. My wife makes dinner—usually something very sensible, you know, grilled chicken, some steamed broccoli, maybe a baked potato—and I eat a completely normal portion when I get home, right before I sit down to start pulling the daily server logs. I haven't lost any weight. My belt is on the exact same notch it’s been on since 2018. 

So, no, the stress of this whole... situation... it hasn't impacted my stomach or my appetite in the slightest. My body needs fuel to keep my mind sharp. If I stopped eating, my blood sugar would drop, my focus would slip, and I'd miss a discrepancy in the logs. That's exactly the kind of opening they're waiting for. I simply can't afford a cognitive dip. So I make sure I eat regularly, consistently, and without any issues. No changes at all.
Have you felt unusually anxious or irritable over the past fourteen months?

Anxious? Irritable? No, I wouldn't use those words. I really wouldn't. You see, anxiety implies a fear of the unknown, doesn't it? It implies a sort of... a nervous anticipation that something bad might happen without any real proof that it will. It's an irrational state. But I don't operate in the realm of the unknown. I operate in the realm of hard data. I have the server logs. When you know exactly what the variables are, when you can literally trace the exact routing algorithms Dave and the management team are using to funnel the complex, tier-three network failure tickets to my specific queue, there's absolutely no room for anxiety. It’s just a math problem at that point. You don't get anxious about a math problem; you just solve it. You gather the data, you isolate the variables, and you compile the proof. So, no, no anxiety. I'm completely calm because I know exactly what they're doing. 

And as for irritable... well. I mean, look at it this way. If you asked my wife, she might say I’m a little more focused lately, maybe a little less talkative during the evening news because I'm running queries in my head, but irritable? No. Irritability implies an emotional reaction, a loss of control, a short temper. I don't lose control. 

Do I find it frustrating when Dave—who, by the way, still doesn't seem to understand the basic functional difference between a MAC address and an IP address, despite being the so-called floor manager—when he makes a snide comment by the water cooler about my ticket resolution times? Of course I find it intellectually offensive. It's objectively absurd that he's criticizing my metrics when he's the one artificially inflating them. But I don't snap at him. I don't raise my voice or get testy. I just smile, I nod, and I make a mental note of the exact timestamp so I can cross-reference his behavior with the dispatch logs when I get home. 

If anything, this whole situation over the past fourteen months has made me significantly more patient. More methodical. You simply cannot let emotion cloud your judgment when you're building a statistical case of this magnitude. If I got irritable, if I let them get under my skin, I might rush my analysis. I might make a syntax error in my spreadsheet formulas, and that is exactly the kind of unforced error they are hoping I'll make. So, I keep my emotions completely flat. Purely analytical. No anxiety, no irritability. Just absolute, unwavering focus on the data.
Have you ever felt like things around you weren't real?

Not real? Like... like a dream, or some kind of simulation? No. No, absolutely not. I would say it’s exactly the opposite, doctor. Everything is incredibly, undeniably real. You see, I work in a field where reality is... well, it's binary. It's ones and zeros. It's measurable. When people talk about feeling disconnected from reality, I always assume they must not work with physical infrastructure. 

Take my daily environment, for instance. There is nothing unreal about a server room. When you walk in there, the ambient temperature is exactly 68 degrees. The hum of the cooling fans is a constant 70 decibels. You can literally feel the vibration of the hard drives through the raised floor tiles. If a switch goes down, it’s not some abstract concept; it’s a physical piece of hardware, usually a Cisco Catalyst sitting in rack three, unit twelve, with a blinking amber light that tells you exactly what the hardware fault is. 

So, when you ask if things feel unreal... I mean, how could they? The data I’m collecting, the logs I’m pulling every single night to track how Dave and the others are manipulating the dispatch queue—those are hard, tangible files. They have file sizes, they have creation dates, they have cryptographic checksums that verify their integrity. You can't fake a checksum, doctor. It’s a mathematical certainty. If things weren't real, if this was all just some sort of illusion, I wouldn't be able to export the server logs to a CSV file and run pivot tables on them, would I? 

I think... well, I think maybe people who don't understand technology might feel like the world isn't real because they don't know how things work under the hood. They just click a button on their screen and magic happens. But I know the routing protocols. I know the exact copper wire and fiber optic pathways the data takes to get from point A to point B. My reality is grounded in pure, unadulterated facts. The tickets Dave sends me, the timestamps, the sheer, statistically impossible volume of tier-three requests landing on my desk—it’s all documented. It’s all very, very real. Honestly, I wish some of it wasn't real. It would certainly save me a lot of time on my spreadsheet analysis. But no. I am completely anchored in reality. I have the data to prove it.
Have you felt guilty about anything recently?

Guilty? About what? No, no, I... I really don't see how guilt factors into this equation at all. You see, doctor, guilt is—well, it's the emotional byproduct of a moral or professional failing, isn't it? It’s what happens when you know you’ve violated a protocol, or neglected a duty, or made an error that negatively impacted the system. And my protocols are ironclad. 

I mean, let's just look at the facts. I log in at 7:45 AM every single day. I don't take sick days. Back in... I think it was late November, when I had a rather severe sinus infection, I still used the VPN to remote in from home and cleared forty-two tickets before noon. My personal resolution rate is impeccable. So professionally? My conscience is completely spotless. I haven't done a single thing to feel guilty about. 

If anything, I am the one holding the entire infrastructure together while they actively try to bury me. If anyone should be sitting in that chair talking to you about guilt, it should be Dave and the management team. They’re the ones intentionally misconfiguring the load balancers to route all the critical network failures to my specific workstation. But, of course, to feel guilty, you have to actually care about the integrity of the system, and I'm fairly certain Dave doesn't even know what the word integrity means in a network context. 

But as for me, no. When you know you are operating entirely within the parameters of the truth, when you have the raw data—the exported logs, the timestamps, the packet loss reports—proving that you are the target of a coordinated, algorithmic assault on your performance metrics... well, there's simply no bandwidth for guilt. I haven't committed any errors. I haven't wronged anyone. I am just doing my job, and frankly, I'm doing it exceptionally well under statistically impossible circumstances. So, no. No guilt whatsoever. My conscience is as clean as a freshly formatted hard drive.
Have you noticed any changes in your relationships with family or friends over the past fourteen months?

Changes? No, I... I wouldn't say there have been changes in any measurable sense. I mean, people might assume—and I suppose this is a common psychological trap for the layman—they might assume that because I am currently having to manage this... this massive, coordinated issue with the ticket rotation and the constant, unwarranted audits they keep throwing at my queue, that my personal life or my social interactions would somehow degrade. But that’s simply not the case. A well-designed system doesn't just collapse because one node is under a DDoS attack, doctor. You isolate the issue. 

Outside of this specific issue with the ticket rotation and the audits, everything in my life is operating at absolute peak efficiency. My wife, for instance—I mentioned her earlier—our relationship is perfectly stable. I still help her with whatever she needs. If the gutters need cleaning, I clean them. If her tablet is experiencing latency issues, I run a diagnostic, flush the DNS, and optimize her network settings. I still keep the entire house in completely working order. 

The bills are paid exactly on time, every single month, down to the day. I actually maintain a dual-entry ledger system I built myself just for our household finances, cross-referenced with our bank's API, so there’s absolutely no disorganization there. Everything is automated, everything is documented. My wife certainly hasn't complained. 

And even at work, regarding my peers... well, if you separate the artificial metrics Dave is trying to manufacture, I still handle all the actual technical parts of my job flawlessly. You can ask anyone on the floor about my physical hardware repairs or my subnet configurations. Not a single person could ever look at my actual output and say my work is sloppy or disorganized. They literally can't. Because it isn't. The cables are tied, the ports are labeled, the documentation is pristine. 

So, no, my relationships, my daily responsibilities... they are completely intact. I don't let the anomalies in the dispatch logs affect my baseline functioning at home or with my colleagues. I compartmentalize it. It’s just another process running in the background, being monitored and logged until I have enough data to expose it.
Have you felt a persistent sadness or hopelessness over the past fourteen months?

Sadness? Hopelessness? No, no, not at all. I mean, hopelessness implies a complete lack of agency, doesn't it? It implies you've just... thrown up your hands and accepted a system failure without even trying to run a proper diagnostic. And that is simply not how I operate, doctor. When a server goes offline, or a network switch suddenly starts dropping half its packets, you don't just sit on the floor and cry about it. You don't get sad. You run a traceroute. You check the event viewer. You find the exact point of failure and you document it. 

So, over the past fourteen months—which, and I’m sure you’d find this interesting, aligns perfectly with when they rolled out the new ticketing system and Dave got his hands on the administrative privileges—I haven't felt hopeless for a single millisecond. Have I been frustrated? Well, of course. It is incredibly frustrating to see a statistically impossible spike in tier-three escalations routed exclusively to my specific workstation while the rest of the team sits around handling simple password resets. Any logical person would be annoyed by that level of blatant, calculated manipulation. 

But hopeless? Absolutely not. Because I have the tools to expose it. Hopelessness is for end-users. It's for people who just stare at a blue screen and don't know what the error code means. I know exactly what the error code is here. I’ve actually written a custom Python script—well, it’s a series of scripts, really, running on a secure virtual machine I provisioned on my home network—that scrapes the dispatch logs every fifteen minutes. It cross-references the time a ticket is submitted with the exact millisecond Dave assigns it to my queue. I am compiling a dataset so comprehensive, so mathematically airtight, that when I finally present it to the regional director, they won't have any choice but to launch a full investigation. 

So you see, I really don't have the time or the bandwidth to be sad. I am actively troubleshooting the problem. I'm building a case. Sadness just doesn't factor into the workflow when you're this close to uncovering the root cause of the issue. My morale is perfectly fine.
Have you noticed any changes in your daily routines or activities outside of work over the past fourteen months?

I feel like we are looping back to the exact same data points here, doctor, but I am happy to reiterate it for your notes. Like I was just saying a few minutes ago when you asked about my wife and my colleagues—my baseline routines haven't degraded at all. 

I am a creature of habit, and my habits are highly optimized. So, outside of having to constantly monitor and document this... this entirely fabricated issue with the ticket rotation and the endless, baseless audits they keep throwing at me, the rest of my life runs like absolute clockwork. I still keep the house in perfect order. My weekend routine hasn't deviated by so much as a half-hour in the last fourteen months. Saturday mornings, I check the HVAC filters, I inspect the perimeter of the property for any maintenance issues, I manage the landscaping. 

And as I mentioned before, I still pay all the bills exactly on time using the automated ledger I built. I still help my wife with her daily needs, whether she needs me to run out to the hardware store or recalibrate her devices. She hasn't noticed any drop in my reliability, because there hasn't been one. 

Even extending that to the physical, technical parts of my job—which I know you asked about my life outside of work, but it's all part of my daily functioning—no one is walking around saying my work is sloppy or disorganized. They can't. The physical output is flawless. 

So, no, my routines haven't changed. The only anomaly in my day-to-day schedule is the extra time I am forced to spend compiling the data to prove I'm being targeted by Dave's algorithmic manipulation. But I don't let that bleed into my baseline activities. I isolate the variable. The rest of the system—my life, my routines, my household chores—remains one hundred percent operational.
Have you ever felt like you were in a dream or a fog, detached from the world around you?

A dream? Or a fog? No, I... I really don't think you're grasping how my mind operates, doctor. A fog implies a lack of clarity, a degradation of the cognitive feed. Like a... like a bad connection dropping frames, or severe latency on a remote desktop session. I don't experience packet loss in my perception of reality.
